The 4-8 week median has no published source, so it should go and readers should be sent to the live guide.

column5: The child usually receives a Bridging Visa E (BVE) if they enter Australia after lodging but before a decision is made.
column7: A 101 application must be made from outside Australia, and the child generally must be outside Australia when the visa is granted. Because it is not an onshore application, it does not give the child a bridging visa. If the child visits Australia while it is being processed, they need another visa, such as a visitor visa, and must comply with its conditions.
column8: Migration Regulations 1994 Sch 1 item 1108(3)(aa) (Child (Migrant) (Class AH): applicant must be outside Australia); Sch 2 cl 101.411 (applicant must be outside Australia at grant, subject to the COVID concession in 101.411(2)); Sch 2 cl 050.212(3) and cl 010.211(2) (BVE/BVA require a valid application made in Australia for a visa that can be granted in Australia) - LEGEND stack 02-10-2026

column5: The 820 visa holder receives a bridging visa while the application is processed.
column7: When the 820/801 application is lodged in Australia while the applicant still holds their 300 visa, they are normally granted a Bridging Visa A. It comes into effect when the 300 visa ends and lets them stay in Australia until the 820 is decided.
column8: Migration Regulations 1994 Sch 2 cl 010.211(2) (BVA where a valid onshore application for a substantive visa is made while holding a substantive visa) and cl 010.511(1) (BVA comes into effect on grant or when the substantive visa ceases; permits stay until the substantive visa decision) - LEGEND stack 02-10-2026
column9: The bridging visa attaches to the pending 820/801 application, not to an 820 holder; because the applicant holds a 300 at lodgement, the BVA sits behind the 300 and takes effect when it ends. Wording names the BVA and keeps 'normally' because grant still depends on a valid onshore application.

column5: If the family needs the parent to have work rights and Medicare during the wait, the contributory subclass 864 (or the offshore 143 or 173) may be more suitable, despite the higher charge.
column7: If the family needs the parent to work, or to have Medicare, while waiting, the two-stage contributory route may suit better despite the higher charge. Subclass 884 (applied for in Australia) and subclass 173 (granted outside Australia) holders have no work restriction and can enrol in Medicare. A bridging visa granted with an onshore 804 or 864 application usually carries the same work conditions as the visa held at lodgement, so a parent who applied while on a visitor visa generally cannot work while waiting, and 804 and 864 applicants are generally not eligible for Medicare until the visa is granted.
column8: Sch 2 cl 173.611-173.612 and cl 884.6 (no work condition on 173/884); cl 173.411 (173 granted outside Australia); cl 010.611(4) (BVA carries work conditions such as 8101 that applied to the visa held at application) - LEGEND stack 02-10-2026. Medicare: Services Australia 'If you're an Australian permanent resident' (parent visa applicants generally not eligible until grant unless RHCA, or for 143/864 if they held a 173/884) and 'If you're a temporary resident covered by a Ministerial Order' (Contributory Parent visas 173, 143, 884, 864); Services Australia Operational Blueprint 011-23032034. LEGEND does not cover Medicare.
column9: The current text wrongly says an 864 gives work rights and Medicare while waiting; it is the temporary 173/884 that do. 'Generally has no work rights' was too absolute: BVA work conditions mirror the visa held at lodgement, so the wording ties it to the common visitor-visa case.

column5: The Balance of Family test is assessed at the time of decision on the application (when the visa is being granted), not necessarily at the time of lodgement.
column7: The balance of family test is assessed at the time of application for the 103, 143, 173, 804, 864 and 884 visas. The family situation when the application is lodged is what counts, so a later change, such as a sibling migrating to Australia after lodgement, will not fix a test that was failed at lodgement. Parents who already hold a 173 or 884 when they apply for the 143 or 864 do not need to meet the test again.
column8: Sch 2 cl 103.213, 143.213, 173.213, 804.214, 864.214 and 884.213 - each in the Division 'Criteria to be satisfied at time of application' and not repeated in the time-of-decision Division; reg 1.05 (test); PAM3: Sch2 Parent visas s3.3.3.3 ('Generally, the balance of family test must only be met at the time of application', with the 173/884 and substituted 600 exceptions) - LEGEND stack 02-10-2026
column9: Confirmed for all six subclasses; the current 'time of decision' statement is wrong. Added the 173/884 exception from cl 143.213/864.214 and PAM3 so the statement is not overbroad (substituted 600 holders are also exempt but are rare enough to leave off the page).

Home Affairs asks for the AoS near the end of processing, once the application has been released from the queue and other criteria are met, and it must be accepted before the visa can be granted. Do not arrange the bond until Services Australia asks for it in writing.
column8: Sch 2 cl 143.228 (AoS accepted by the Secretary of Social Services - time of decision); PAM3: Div1.2/reg1.03 - Assurance of Support (AoS), s3.5.1 (request after other criteria met and after queue release) and s3.6 (AoS bond administered by Services Australia); PAM3: Sch2 Parent visas s3.4.3 (AoS mandatory for 103, 143, 804, 864; not 173/884) - LEGEND stack 02-10-2026; Services Australia bank guarantee and term deposit page.

column5: The parent can apply for the 870 while also being in the permanent visa queue. The 870 requires an approved sponsor and health insurance for the duration of the stay. There is a 90-day gap required outside Australia before applying for a second 870 in some circumstances
column7: A parent who has already lodged a permanent parent visa application can still apply for, and be granted, an 870 to visit Australia while that application is processed. However, a parent who has applied for or holds an 870, or who held one and has not left Australia since it ended, cannot make a valid application for any permanent or temporary parent visa. The 870 requires an approved parent sponsor and adequate health insurance. A further 870 must generally be lodged from outside Australia, and unless there are exceptional circumstances it cannot be granted until the parent has been outside Australia for at least 90 consecutive days since leaving after their last 870.
column8: Sch 2 Part 870 (cl 870.221-870.229, all time-of-decision criteria; none bars a pending permanent parent application; cl 870.223 = 90 consecutive days rule; cl 870.224 health insurance); Sch 1 item 1239(3)(b),(e) (870 validity: must not hold an 870; must be outside Australia unless permitted); Sch 1 items 1124(3)(ac), 1124A(3)(bb), 1130(3)(bb), 1130A(3)(ca), 1221(3)(aa), 1221A(3)(ca) (parent visa validity: must not hold an 870 and, if held one, must have left Australia since it ceased); PAM3: Sch2 Visa 870 - Subclass 870 (Sponsored Parent (Temporary)) visa, s3.2 Restrictions and s3.6.3 - LEGEND stack 02-10-2026
column9: PAM3 s3.2 expressly confirms a person with a pending permanent parent application may apply for and be granted an 870, and that 870 applicants, holders and former holders who have not left Australia cannot validly apply for 103/804/143/864/173/884. Note the Sch 1 text bars only holders (and former holders still onshore); 'applied for' follows PAM3 and Home Affairs and is the safer statement.

column5: Yes. A parent can simultaneously hold a subclass 870 visa (allowing them to live in Australia) and have a subclass 143 Contributory Parent permanent visa application in the queue. This is a common strategy
column7: Yes, if the permanent application is lodged first. A parent with a pending permanent parent visa application, such as a 143, can apply for and be granted an 870 to visit Australia while it is processed. It does not work the other way: a parent who has applied for or holds an 870, or who held one and has not left Australia since it ended, cannot lodge a 143 or any other parent visa. Families wanting both should get advice on the order of applications before lodging anything.
column8: Sch 2 Part 870 (no criterion about pending parent applications); Sch 1 item 1130(3)(bb) (143 validity - must not hold an 870; former holders must have left Australia) and equivalent items 1124, 1124A, 1130A, 1221, 1221A; PAM3: Sch2 Visa 870 s3.2 Restrictions (note: a person who has already made a permanent Parent visa application may apply for and be granted an SPTV) - LEGEND stack 02-10-2026
column9: PAM3 confirms the 'permanent first, then 870' sequence; the current 'Yes ... common strategy' is wrong if read as allowing a 143 to be lodged while holding an 870. Starting with 'Yes, if...' keeps the FAQ answer direct while stating the order.

column5: it is typically 9 working days for onshore decisions
column7: for a protection visa refusal you must apply within 28 days after you are notified of the decision (or 14 days if you are in immigration detention on the day you are notified), and the ART has no power to extend this time limit. Refusals on character or security grounds follow different rules, so always check your decision letter
column8: Migration Act 1958 s 347(3) (application must be made within 14 days after notification if the applicant is in immigration detention on the day notified, otherwise within 28 days); s 347(5) (ART Act s 19 extension power does not apply to reviewable protection decisions); s 338A (reviewable protection decision includes a decision to refuse a protection visa); s 347A(5) (applicant must be physically in the migration zone); s 500(1)(c) and (6B) (refusals relying on s 5H(2), 36(1C) or 36(2C), and s 501 decisions, are reviewed under s 500 with separate rules, e.g. 9 days for s 501 decisions). LEGEND stack 02-10-2026.
column9: Since the ART commenced, s 347(3) sets 28 days (14 days if in detention when notified) and s 347(5) removes any ART power to extend; the old '9 working days' figure has no basis for ordinary protection refusals. Character/security-based refusals go through s 500 with different limits, hence the caveat.

column8: Migration Regulations 1994 Sch 1 item 1128(3)(b) (Resident Return (Class BB), subclasses 155 and 157): 'The applicant may be in or outside Australia, but not in immigration clearance.' Also Sch 2 cl 157.411 (applicant may be in or outside Australia, but not in immigration clearance, at time of grant). LEGEND stack 02-10-2026.
column9: Item 1128 covers both 155 and 157 and allows the applicant to be in or outside Australia (not in immigration clearance) at lodgement; cl 157.411 mirrors this at grant. The 'offshore only' statement is wrong.

column5: There is no Skills in Demand levy (SAF levy) requirement for the 407
column7: There is no Skilling Australians Fund (SAF) levy for the 407
column8: Migration Act 1958 s 140ZM (nomination training contribution charge applies only to nominations of a kind prescribed by the regulations); Migration Regulations 1994 reg 5.42 (prescribes nominations under s 140GB(1)(b) for Subclass 457, 482 (Skills in Demand / Temporary Skill Shortage) and 494 holders/applicants, and Subclass 186 and 187 visas only - Subclass 407 is not prescribed). Charge imposed by the Migration (Skilling Australians Fund) Charges Act 2018 (s 7). LEGEND stack 02-10-2026.
column9: The SAF levy is the 'nomination training contribution charge' under s 140ZM, and reg 5.42 prescribes only 457/482/494 and 186/187 nominations, so a 407 nomination attracts no levy. 'Skills in Demand' is the name of the 482 visa, not the levy, so the current wording is wrong.

column5: Visitor visa decisions are generally not reviewable at the ART (they are merits-review excluded).
column7: Some visitor visa refusals can be reviewed by the ART. If you applied in Australia, a refusal is generally reviewable, as long as the decision was not made while you were in immigration clearance and you are still in Australia when you apply for review. If you applied from outside Australia, a refusal is only reviewable where you were coming to visit an Australian citizen or permanent resident parent, spouse, de facto partner, child, brother or sister whose details were included in your application. In that case the relative applies to the ART. Check your refusal letter, which states whether review is available and the time limit.
column8: Migration Act 1958 s 338(2) (refusal of a visa that can be granted in the migration zone, applied for in the migration zone, not decided in immigration clearance, other than s 501 decisions, is reviewable); s 338(7) (offshore refusal reviewable where a criterion is intention to visit an Australian citizen/PR parent, spouse, de facto partner, child, brother or sister and the relative's particulars are in the application); s 347A(1)(c) (relative applies for s 338(7) decisions); s 347A(2) (applicant must be in the migration zone for s 338(2) decisions). Migration Regulations 1994 Sch 2 cl 600.221(a) (Tourist stream) and cl 600.231(a) (Sponsored Family stream) contain the visit-a-relative criterion; cl 600.412 (offshore applicants must be outside Australia at grant). LEGEND stack 02-10-2026.
column9: Both the current text and the proposed 'most visitor refusals are not reviewable' understate review rights: onshore 600 refusals are reviewable under s 338(2), and offshore Tourist and Sponsored Family stream refusals are reviewable by the relative under s 338(7) where the relative's details were in the application. Other offshore visitor refusals (e.g. Business Visitor, ADS, Frequent Traveller) are not reviewable.

column5: Requires legal representation.
column7: Legal representation is strongly recommended.
column8: Migration Act 1958 Part 8 (ss 476-486) confers judicial review jurisdiction and contains no requirement that an applicant be legally represented (LEGEND stack 02-10-2026). The Federal Circuit and Family Court confirms parties may appear as unrepresented litigants. Not a LEGEND policy point.
column9: Nothing in Part 8 of the Act or the Court's rules makes representation mandatory, and the FCFCOA publishes guidance for self-represented litigants, so 'requires legal representation' overstates the position. Recommending representation is accurate and appropriate.
